passage:
Jin had spent two years building a small app in Seoul that helped bakeries plan their morning batches. One Tuesday, Chidi, who ran a supplier account, forwarded a screenshot: a much larger company had launched nearly the same features and was giving them away at half the price.

Jin's face went hot. For an hour he typed and deleted an angry post about copycats, then closed the laptop.

That night he called five of his bakery customers instead. Most of them said they stayed because of the way he answered their calls at six in the morning and adjusted the app to their tiny shops. "The big one doesn't know our ovens," one baker said.

Chidi came by on Friday. "What can't they copy?"

Jin wrote three words on a sticky note: "Listening. Small. Fast." He stuck it above his screen and turned back to work.

qa.q: What did the bakery app help bakeries plan?
qa.a: It helped bakeries plan their morning batches.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when he typed and deleted the angry post?
qa.a: Jin was angry, shown by his hot face and the long stretch of typing and deleting, and stopped himself from posting.

qa.q: What did Jin do instead of complaining publicly?
qa.a: He phoned five bakery customers, learned why they stayed, and focused on what the big company could not copy: listening, small scale and speed.

qa.q: How might a bakery owner see the bigger company's cheaper app?
qa.a: A bakery owner may find the lower price tempting, but may still feel the big company does not understand a tiny shop's ovens or hours.

grounding: A bigger competitor copies Jin's product and undercuts prices; Jin feels anger, then focuses on customers he serves better instead of complaining publicly.

passage:
"Did you see it, Vikas? The grocery giant's new pickle box. Same jars, same subscription, same regional recipes. Half our price."
"I saw it at six this morning. I've been angry since."
"Kalyani, they're a massive grocery company. They copied our whole idea."
"I know. My first thought was to post their packaging next to ours and call them thieves."
"Should we?"
Kalyani paused. "It'll feel good for a day. Then we look bitter, and they don't care."
"So what, then?"
"What can't they copy? Our aunties. Every jar is made by a named woman in Kolhapur, with her story on the label. Customers write to them. They love that."
"And the chat group where people ask Radha-maushi for recipes."
"Exactly. They can copy a jar, not that."
"So we double down on the people."
"And our top two hundred customers. Personal notes this month."
Vikas nodded slowly. "Still angry."
"Me too. Let's use it."

qa.q: Where are the jars made, according to Kalyani?
qa.a: In Kolhapur, each by a named woman with her story on the label.

qa.q: How did Kalyani and Vikas feel when they saw the copy?
qa.a: They felt angry, with Kalyani tempted to publicly call the competitor thieves.

qa.q: What did they decide to focus on instead of complaining publicly?
qa.a: The things that can't be copied: the named cooks, the recipe chat group, and personal notes to their top two hundred customers.

qa.q: How might their loyal customers see the bigger company's cheaper jars?
qa.a: Loyal customers may still prefer the original, valuing the personal stories and connection more than the lower price.

grounding: A bigger competitor copies the product and undercuts prices; the founders feel angry but focus on customers and what cannot be copied instead of trashing the rival.

passage:
I'm Irfan, and last year a big electronics chain launched a phone-repair service that looked exactly like ours, same doorstep pickup, same three-day promise, at a lower price. I remember reading their ad in the metro and feeling my ears go hot. We'd built that in Lucknow over three years.
That week I wrote a long angry post about "corporate thieves". Mehak, my co-founder, read it before I hit send. "Who is this for?" she asked. I didn't have a good answer.
So we deleted it and called twenty of our regular customers instead. What did they value? Not the price. It was that our technicians explained the repair in Hindi, didn't upsell, and fixed old phones the chain refused to touch.
We doubled down on that. Old models. Plain explanations. Six months later, we'd lost some customers to the chain. But the ones who stayed brought their parents.

qa.q: How many regular customers did Irfan and Mehak call?
What was Irfan feeling when reading the competitor's ad in the metro?
qa.a: Irfan felt angry and wronged, ears going hot, after building the service over three years.

qa.q: Which choice helped more than the angry post, and why?
qa.a: Asking customers what they valued and focusing on it, old phones and plain explanations, which the chain couldn't easily copy.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt reading the angry post?
qa.a: Mehak was probably worried it would make them look bitter, and calm enough to ask who it was really for.

grounding: A bigger competitor copies the service at a lower price; the protagonist feels angry but focuses on what customers value and what cannot be copied.
